utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one minor matter. Yesterday we referred to a milinfosum dated the 21st of April, 1993. I had thought that it had been introduced by the Prosecution with a "Z" number. Apparently it has not, so I would just like to have that marked as the next Defence exhibit by the registrar, if that's possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D159/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be speaking Croatian in this case. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and I come from Rijeka, and today with my colleague Mr. Mikulicic from Zagreb, I represent Mr. Cerkez. Due to differences in language, we must both take care to make a short break to give the interpreters time to finish their interpretation. Thank you very much. Mr. Stewart, from your testimony in the Blaskic case, I gather that there is no doubt that Blaskic was the immediate superior to Cerkez in the course of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think that he was a superior to Mr. Cerkez. I don't quite know whether he was the immediate superior to Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that Blaskic was the commander of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that Cerkez was a brigade commander that comes under that zone?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is also my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Blaskic's headquarters was in the hotel in the centre of the town of Vitez, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Cerkez' headquarters was a couple of hundred metres away in another building, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that. I don't think -- I'm not sure whether I visited that headquarter, unless it was in the town hall, which I did visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I do believe that from general information, you do know that his headquarters was in the town of Vitez, regardless of the fact that you may not know the precise location.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is correct, and I normally met Mr. Cerkez around about the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the summary given to us by the Prosecution and which served as a guideline for the examination-in-chief, I think due to some error, point 9 was not read out of the summary, and I should like to read it. It says: "According to the Prosecution, can you confirm that you agree with the statement," and let me read it in English, "... consider Cerkez to be an apparently decent enough, likable man, on the face of it, who was commander of Vitez town."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That is exactly what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But could we devote a little time to this assessment of yours that Cerkez was the commander of the town? First of all, did he ever tell you that or explain that to you? Did you ever ask him what his exact position was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I think that most likely it became apparent that that seemed to be the case. I don't think I would have asked him directly, that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: To make things quite clear, let me ask you whether you ever saw a written document or third person addressing Cerkez in a certain way which would confirm that he was the commander of the town.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I believe it was the assessment of some of my liaison officers. I believe it was the assessment of the intelligence section. I believe that it was my opinion that he was probably influential in the HVO organisation. "Influential," by that I mean I imagined and thought him to be the commander. But later on, he had moved, and I thought he went to Novi Travnik as well. But it was just an impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In your opinion and in view of your experience, and when I ask a witness for an opinion, I think that is acceptable, from the military standpoint, what would it mean for a military commander to be the commander of the town? Would that mean that he was commander of the civilian authorities in town as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think the organisation of the so-called, as we described it, Vitez government was a combination of many different authorities, and that just didn't apply to the military and the civilian. There was also police -- military police there who complicated the matter. They had made it very difficult for us to assess exactly who was responsible for what. For example, on one occasion my sentries at my fuel dump were attacked by people in a car. The car fired shots at my soldiers, and then they reported the fact to me. I was in the operations room, and I was angry with them because they had not been quick enough, quick enough to fire back, because it's bad for professional soldiers to lose the initiative. Unfortunately for the people in the car, they decided to have another go and they drove past again. One man died in consequence, I'm sad to say. But when I went to the Vitez government the next day, I was directed to the military police or the police. This was not Cerkez. And the police chief complained to me that my soldiers had fired. But I gave him a full report, minute by minute, of exactly what had happened and said, "It's your responsibility to stop HVO soldiers," and it was one, "from attacking my soldiers, and they deserved what they got, although I'm sad, of course, that one of them subsequently died in hospital." But there is an example, I contend, that makes it very difficult for people who, like myself, have come into the area largely ignorant, and we accept that, largely ignorant, but doing our very best to try and work out a situation, at the same time having to deal with a very hostile environment. So I say that because, you know, your question was, "Was Mr. Cerkez responsible for everything military in the town?" I suspect he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] I will speak Croatian. I beg your pardon. So I take it that this term, "commander of the town," does not cover any broader competencies beyond the military, in the sense that you use it here.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I took it that he was the commander of the HVO in the town area of Vitez, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the example you have given, it seems to me that there is also no doubt that you made a distinction within the HVO between the military and the civilian sections.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: In some cases, yes. It depended on what we found. The problem was to try and find the correct authorities when going to make a complaint. For example, you know, when a vehicle was hijacked, I didn't know who to go to, so in one case I went to the mayor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mention was made here, and with the assistance of the registry, could we find D36/2. You will see the document in a minute, but by way of introduction, let me say that a document was mentioned linked to a meeting held on the 16th of April, 1993 organised by your second in command, Mr. Bryan Watters, in the early afternoon of the 16th of April. Could you please take a look at that document to refresh your memory. It was mentioned indirectly yesterday, this first HVO officer, Marko Prskalo was wounded coming out of the Warrior near the hotel returning from the meeting, but that is not relevant just now. What I would like to draw your attention to is that in the paragraph after listing the names, one can see that the subject of the meeting was the conflict in Vitez; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From this document, it is also evident that there were two parties to the negotiations; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO side, the Croatian side, was represented by officers Marko Prskalo and Zoran Pilicic, and we know without any doubt, and we will produce many exhibits to confirm this, that they represent Blaskic, that both of them are members of the Blaskic command. Do you know this and can you confirm that? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't recognise the names; therefore, I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names and positions of the representatives of the BH army side? And their positions are stated here in full, Mr. Dzidic and Mr. Sivro.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think I remember Mr. Dzidic. Mr. Sivro, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, judging by the titles and what you can remember, there is no doubt that representatives of the BH army are representatives of the local military forces quartered in Vitez; can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That looks likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We don't need that document anymore. If I may go on to another topic. Colonel, I have been told that as a sign of goodwill you made a gift of a wooden coat of arms of the Cheshire Regiment to Cerkez, and even later on when your book was published, that you sent him a copy. May I ask you, was that something that you did as a rule in your dealings with the officers you had contact with during your tour of duty in Bosnia, or was this some kind of a sign of appreciation for those you considered to be acceptable, correct people, decent people.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think it was a mixture of both. But with regard to Mr. Cerkez, I believe Mr. Cerkez to be a decent man and an honourable man, and I never saw anything in his behaviour whatsoever that caused me to change that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Let me now go on to another issue with a few questions only. In your testimony in the Blaskic case, and I'm referring to an issue covered by pages 23823 through to 23824, the next page, let me briefly remind you that the Defence in the Blaskic case put to you questions comparing the HVO to NATO standards. First of all, he spoke about the chain of command structure, professionalism, the chain of command and control, then about the training and discipline standards, ranks, and other things. Do you remember what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or perhaps we need to show that part of the transcript to the witness. It was tendered yesterday as Z2791.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't need to see it, I can remember, unless there's some tricky point in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you do remember the issue, my question is a simple one. This assessment that you gave in the Blaskic case in answer to a question by the Defence, does that also apply to the unit known as the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Of course it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There's no difference.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. I mean, it's very difficult for people to suddenly go to war from a civilian situation, and it was clear to me that many of the leaders, maybe I won't use the word "officers," and I don't mean that in a derogatory way, many of the leaders of the HVO and the BiH were cast into the situation by the circumstances of the time. Just let me take a case -- a point that has nothing to do with it. The commander, the leader of the BiH in the town of Turbe was a schoolmaster one day and a leader the next. This could well have been the case with Mr. Cerkez or, indeed -- well, as we know with Dario Kordic. You know, I have sympathy and sadness for that situation for them. So, of course, they didn't have the same kind of background or the same kind of discipline, the same kind of rules, but what they tried to do was to adapt what they could in the circumstances of the time, and by no means do I imply in this a criticism of any man's courage. I mean, I'm just talking about procedures and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Among other things, with respect to this issue, you said at one point [In English] "... at the time his officer said that the rank and file, most certainly the majority of them had not ..." You include Cerkez there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know Mr. Cerkez's background. I suspect every single man of a certain age had done military service in the JNA, but that doesn't necessarily qualify them to lead a war with limited resources, with no organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, to round off this topic with a final question, in your contacts, and I'm not referring to your personal contacts only but those made by your liaison officers as well, did you obtain information about the level of development of the organisation of the Vitez Brigade? I bear in mind the fact that it was established only some 20 days prior to the conflict. Did you learn that this was a brigade in the process of formation, that it was still not a fully developed and organised brigade; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't know it. I suspected it. I suspected that the reason -- and I can tell you that the reason why we went to Blaskic the whole time is that I knew him to be a regular officer of the JNA, as indeed Mr. Merdan was, and therefore would understand the requirements. I tended to go to that kind of person because, apart from anything else, the rules of war would be totally understandable to a regular officer. Mr. Cerkez tended to be co-located in my mind at Mr. Blaskic's -- or Colonel Blaskic's headquarters, and of course I would deal with Mr. Cerkez, and I don't mean "deal with," go and see Mr. Cerkez in the absence of Colonel Blaskic because I assumed him to be someone in authority in the HVO within the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, may I take it from that, or rather does that concur with a military principle that I understand very well as a layman, and that is that if in an area we have two commanders of different levels, a higher and a lower level one, clearly the higher level commander is the most important, and as a third party, we would go and deal with this higher level commander. Would that be part of this picture that you have just portrayed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, but the military principle is of delegated command. If you think of an admiral on a battleship, he's often not the captain of the ship. In certain areas of responsibility like action, the admiral may well be told to go to his cabin and shut up while the captain deals with the enemy, and I'm using a surface fleet analogy to make my point. It may well be that there is a situation where Blaskic is -- his headquarters is superimposed on the organisation, but actually the day-to-day running of the brigade is left to the appropriate commander, and that is the way I assumed brigades in the HVO worked. Blaskic could not command everything directly, he had to go through subordinate commanders and also had to delegate responsibility to those commanders as best he could in the circumstances that this was a nascent, a very young military force. So, therefore, for example, a problem with a roadblock outside Vitez, it would properly be dealt with by going to see Mario Cerkez. A problem with the whole of the Lasva Valley apparently going to war, it must be dealt with by going to see Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But having used this as an illustration, for the sake of illustration when talking about this example that you mentioned, a roadblock in the town or in its vicinity, you would normally address the brigade commander. You would go to the commander to which the troops at the roadblock are accountable, of course, on condition that we know whom they belong to. If it is the police, we would go to the police commander; if it is the brigade, the brigade commander; if it is the Bosnian army, we would go to the Bosnian army commander. We agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, but we would start by going to see the roadblock itself to say, "Why are you doing this and who has given you orders to do it?" And then we would follow up the chain of command. It's a standard way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is one other issue that I would like to discuss from your previous testimony on page 23826. You stated, in response to a question which was as follows: [In English] "... on the 16th of April, as of the evening of the 15th?" [Interpretation] Your answer to that question was as follows: [In English] "... was because I anticipated that unless the problem in Zenica was resolved, there could be serious repercussions, and I suppose I was right, sadly." That was the answer. [Interpretation] My question for you is the following: You know what the circumstances were at the time. Do you know whether Cerkez had any reason to believe that there would be a war on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: We are talking the 15th of April? We're talking of the date of the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the eve of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think that he would necessarily think that the 16th was going to be the D-Day, the start. I think that the whole of the HVO and the whole of the BiH would have been extremely blind if they hadn't realised there was trouble coming. And going to the next question, if you had one, I don't know how much Mr. Cerkez would have known about any preparations for attacks in the Lasva Valley. I suspect he would -- if he didn't pick up something was going on, I would be surprised. But as to his degree of authority or responsibility for what was happening, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. If I may follow up with a clarification or, rather, a question. From all the BritBat reports and other evidence that we heard here, it follows that there is no basis for conclusion that during the days that preceded the 16th of April, that troops had been reinforced in terms of personnel and equipment. You also spoke about a tension which was due to a range of incidents that took place before that. However, I know that there were no reports about any reinforcement of troops. We do not have such documents. We do not dispose of such evidence. Would you agree with that assessment? One could feel it in the air. However, it was not stated in any of the military documents. Would that concur with your conclusions at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The way I ran my battalion was as follows: I always tried to be in my headquarters at 5.00 each night. At 5.00 each night for at least half an hour, I listened to the reports of the previous 24 hours. We had an intelligence assessment, we had an operational assessment, we had reports from the United Nations agencies and sometimes the International Committee of the Red Cross. The military infosums, which have been produced in evidence so far, I didn't normally read because I wanted to listen to the reports of the people who wrote those things and correct or modify them at that conference. So when they went out, they were normally not with my sighting of them, because I was concerned with actually dealing with matters on the ground, not reporting back. For some days prior to the 15th, there had been serious tension in the whole of the Lasva Valley, and by that I mean going into Novi Travnik, Travnik, Vitez, going down the valley to -- all the way to Kiseljak and into Zenica. There was very great tension there, and tension is sometimes difficult to communicate in reports anyway. But I had given instructions to my liaison officers, who were divided by sectors, and they dealt with areas like Novi Travnik or -- to actually keep in contact with the relevant headquarters, find out if something was going to be happening so that we could try and stop people losing their lives by action immediately, and in any case to report to me instantly if they saw a situation which might develop which would cause people to lose their lives. Those are the instructions that happened prior to the 15th. And it was for this reason that I was in Travnik actually at the time when the Totic kidnapping and murders took place by apparently Mujahedin in Zenica. I was actually walking the streets at the time, talking to soldiers, who were operating on the ground, of the BiH or HVO, if I could find them. So your question, I'm sorry if it's been long-winded in reply, but I wanted to explain the circumstances. Your question is quite right. In the British military information summaries or whatever, the tension would not be communicated, necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, if I may summarise what you have said, according to the way I understand and according to the information that you had at the time, you all felt tension in the air. However, there were no military indications as to the possibility of an oncoming conflict in the following days. Would that be an accurate conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the days prior to the conflict, and you mentioned something to that effect before, the HVO, in the area of Turbe, still held the line together with the Bosnian army, and they had contacts with Lajko Sulejman, a BiH army commander who you mentioned yesterday, I believe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What was worrying me was the apparent withdrawal of HVO forces from the area of Turbe at this time. The HVO and the BiH were disengaging from one another. This was a serious worry to me, because it implied the break-up of the coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that according to the information we have, the HVO had decreased its presence in that area; however, the Vitez part, there was no significant withdrawal in the Vitez area? Would that be your recollection today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I mean there might be a redeployment from Travnik to Vitez, might have been. I'd like to know where the people from Travnik and Turbe went, but I suspect they went to the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we are still in that area, on the first day of the conflict between the Croat side and the Muslim side in Vitez, that is, on the 16th of April, you had just arrived from Zenica on that morning, and you went back to Zenica a couple of hours later. You already told us about that. Can we say that in the town of Vitez and in its surroundings, can we say that there was a chaos in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be accurate. It was just fighting. People were trying to keep off the streets. People were very, very frightened. When I drove through Vitez that day, I remember seeing some bodies. And, of course, I think the 16th was the day that the bomb in the mosque went off in Vitez, which also killed a number of people. And, quite frankly, when you say it was chaos, I would say it was an absolute war zone at the time and no one, absolutely no one, was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, sir. [Interpretation] Yesterday you testified briefly about the road that leads through the valley, and you indicated on the map the road going through the valley and the mountain road from Zenica to Vitez. I have to ask you something about that road. The portion of the road that is going through the valley, linking Zenica and Vitez, of course, goes on in both directions, eastward and westward. As a soldier, would you agree with me that from the strategical point of view, that was a very important road, not only for the Vitez and the Lasva River Valley, not only for Central Bosnia as a whole, but beyond that as well? Could we agree that it was one of the very important routes going westward and eastward through Bosnia, linking up with the roads that lead to the coast and northward towards Croatia? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, that road was not only of a local significance. In the Lasva River Valley, bearing in mind where the town of Vitez is located exactly, again from the strategical point of view, can we say that the army that wishes to control the area has to hold the elevations that surround the town of Vitez and its surroundings? Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: In order to control a route, one must control the whole of the route. Vitez was a part of the route, particularly the bypass, of course, but so too was that you could break a route like that at any point and dislocate it absolutely, as I gave in evidence yesterday with regard to the fact of the roadblock on that road. So, yes, you know, you can talk in terms of big towns on the route that are vital to be held for the route, and Vitez was one, although I have to say the route didn't go necessarily into the centre of Vitez, it bypassed Vitez and still does. So yes and no. You can break a route any way you like. It's like breaking a straw. If you break a straw anywhere along its length, it doesn't join. So I'm not so convinced that it's absolutely essential to say that any one part is superior to any other, in strategic terms. But, yes, you know, I think I understand your question better. Vitez was an important part of Central Bosnia. It was important that if anyone -- you know, whoever held Vitez, it was important for dominating the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And therefore it is important to hold vital peaks around it? As a layman, do I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: It's an old-fashioned concept that you have to hold a vital peak. It doesn't necessarily follow that you have to. But the answer is, in these terms, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One other issue that has been frequently discussed here and I would like to clarify. The British base camp, you said it was located in Vitez or in the surroundings of the town of Vitez. To be specific, the exact location is called Bila; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I apologise for taking too much time for that, but as a person who spent some time there locally, you're familiar with the fact that Nova Bila is another location, a different one?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And one more question in relation to that and then I'm done. Did you know that, administratively-speaking, the town of Bila was under the municipality of Travnik and not the municipality of Vitez, although you did not necessarily have to know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I didn't, actually. I didn't know that, which would explain why people complained so much when after the mosque bomb I took everyone I found to the Travnik hospital. I had complaints from the government of Vitez that I had taken everyone and I hadn't taken the Croats to a Croatian hospital, Bosnian Croat hospital. But that would explain why -- a reason why people would complain to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you talked about an incident involving a kidnapping of a Mercedes that belonged to the Dutch contingent, and you personally intervened at that time and you went to the Vitez Hotel. Is it true that you spoke to Pasko Ljubicic, the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police there, or was it some other unidentified military policeman that you spoke to? Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know the name. I think I went to the Hotel Vitez, and I went to the mayor as well. And then almost immediately, I went to the Mafia, and I had some dealings with the so-called Mafia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, in the hotel, as far as the hotel is concerned, you remember that you were there in order to speak to the military police of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in your prior testimony, in the testimony that you gave in the Blaskic case, you mentioned a couple of times a place referred to as the Swiss Chalet or Bungalow which was situated not far from Ahmici, near the road in the vicinity of Nadioci. I would like to ask you the following: According to a number of documents from the British Battalion, you're probably familiar with the fact that for a very long time the place had been a base for a unit of the HVO military police, that they would gather there frequently, and that this fact is frequently mentioned. Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I know the place exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the soldiers you saw, and you gave a very graphic description of that, you said according to the behaviour of those policemen, one could tell what had happened. While you were speaking about that, you were referring to that particular location, the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I did not know whether they were policemen or what they were. I just know that they exhibited signs of extreme aggression towards me as I drove past.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Past the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Past the Bungalow. And at the time I didn't really understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, thank you very much for your answers. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a matter that might be dealt with now rather than deal with my re-examination in two parts. Perhaps we can go into private session and discuss the procedure -- not private -- yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if it's the matter you were discussing yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- would it not be convenient to deal with that after your re-examination, to re-examine the witness if there is anything arising from cross-examination and then to deal with the new matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Entirely as the Court prefers. I'll deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Stewart, you've been asked a number of questions, but there's been no actual challenge to the conclusions you've reached in respect of Kordic. In light of the things that you've discussed with counsel for the Defence, do your conclusions about Kordic change at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about opinions on some of your liaison officers, and you indicated there might be a difference between the opinions as expressed in the book and the opinions expressed elsewhere. In respect of which liaison officers, I must ask you, does that apply?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I had some excellent liaison officers and I had some poor liaison officers. The excellent liaison officers were generally moved into the situation from a top-class job, and I refer to the likes of Captain Martin Foregrave, and some of the lesser liaison officers who actually took the job because we didn't have anyone else, and I refer to Captain Matthew Dundas-Whatley, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any others who fall into that category?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think in terms of -- not only liaison officers, I had some pretty mediocre officers as well serving with me. I think Dundas-Whatley was probably the weakest in the field as a liaison officer, and I think within my staff I had some other officers whose judgement was sometimes suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. We --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: The reason why I didn't indicate that in the book is because I don't, I'm loyal, and I'm now under oath. In the book, I don't actually run down people if I can avoid it. In a court, I have to give my honest opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can't know which, if any, officers of your battalion may be called by the Defence, just this: If given notice of any officer who may be called, would you be in a position to give your opinion of his abilities and reliability?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I would prefer that to be in closed session --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: -- because, you know, I don't like people being publicly ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you might have asked Blaskic about the chain of command, on several occasions you dealt with that. With the passage of time between yesterday and today, have you any further or better recollection of whether you did, and, if so, what, if anything, he may have said?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, I don't change what I said yesterday. I might have asked him. You see, I got on very well with Mr. Blaskic and, you know, I had no real axe to grind with Mr. Kordic either. These people treated me with dignity and honour, and, you know, I find it rather sad that after that they are in a court of law, I just feel very sad. But, of course, what I feel and actually what they did are two different matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had various passages summarised to you from earlier testimony concerning your understanding of the chain of command. Do you take it from me that at each time, pages 749, 764, and 855, you expressed your conclusions in cautious terms, saying such things as "At times we were confused about the chain of command"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I tried to demonstrate that in testimony this morning, that most of the time I had to make a judgement as to who I would go to. In Vitez, for example, you know, was it the military police? Was it the mayor? Was it the political side? Was it the HVO? I mean, who was representing who as well? It was extremely difficult. I didn't have on arrival a history of organisation in the area. I was thrown into the area almost naked with regard to intelligence, absolutely naked, and we had to do it as we were running, and therefore I didn't have the resources to dedicate to saying, "Right. Let us find out exactly what the organisation of the HVO, BiH is. You know, it's a matter of crucial concern." It never was a matter of crucial concern. The matter of crucial concern to me was to try and stop the situation deteriorating so that people who had died -- my, as the Germans would call it, schwer punct, point of concentrated effort, was that, not trying to work out exactly how Mr. Kordic, Mr. Cerkez, Mr. Blaskic, or anyone else fit into an organisation, unless it was part of that concentrated effort, which perhaps it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which brings me to the next question. You've been asked on several occasions about whether you asked Kordic or others whether they had authority. Was there ever any need to ask the people you were dealing with whether they had authority delegated or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure there was. When I said, "Are you responsible? Can you help me?" Of course I had to ask that kind of question at times, and I don't know when those occasions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if someone presented as having and acted as having authority, was there any need to go on and ask him whether he had it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No, no. I mean, that was enough for me. I mean, going to see Mr. Kordic in Busovaca, you know, I knew Kordic, he was apparently in command, and I didn't waste time worrying about that. You know, I just wanted to get the job done, I just wanted to get things organised so that actually we could carry on and try and stop people dying principally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You had your attention drawn to some extent to the existence of the special brigades, I suppose. You've given an expression yesterday of opinion about the existence of political control or supervision generally. Does what you say about political control and supervision generally apply also to the special brigades?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: God, I hope so. The trouble is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: You know, I really don't know. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- in the interests of time. If you think I'm being unfair, tell the Judges and they will, no doubt, allow you to go on.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about Blaskic's authority to act at Kordic's absence from particular ceasefire discussions. One way or another, do you know yourself whether Blaskic had to refer elsewhere for the decisions he made or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Sometimes he did and sometimes he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've been asked about Merdan and Dusina and Lasva and so on. What was Merdan within the arc of those who were honourable and reliable and those who may be otherwise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Merdan was a man who the HVO considered to be a decent, straight, and honest man, and I think Mr. Kordic would have said that. He certainly suggested that when they were talking on the 20th of October, that he wouldn't deal with anyone else. Merdan had previous experience in the JNA and was known to Blaskic personally prior to the war, and Merdan was in many ways the person I thought was the broker for the BiH. He was the deputy commander of the corps that was based in Zenica. So in the terms of Bosnia at the time, it seemed to me a very personality-driven situation. You know, Merdan for the BiH, Blaskic for the HVO, and that simplified for me the situation. So, you know, if it was an HVO matter, I would generally try to go to Blaskic and if it was a BiH matter, I'd go to Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did each of those fall within your description of decent and honourable men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: That's it. Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the other decent men of the Busovaca Joint Commission, because you've referred to the decent men on the Busovaca Joint Commission, just to help the Judges, can you name those, in your judgement, who fell into that category?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't remember all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: And please don't think I'm implying that Mr. Kordic wasn't a decent man, it's just he wasn't my kind of man. I don't wish to say -- he and I weren't great at hitting it off, I thought, but other officers of mine did hit it off with Mr. Kordic. What I'm trying to say, and I won't be cut off on this, what I'm trying to say is I found it very difficult that people who had treated me well apparently, and the evidence that I saw, were the commanders of such atrocities, and I think that's the real dichotomy that I have always felt and I always will feel. Now I'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Ahmici -- sorry. I'm listening to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, will you have an eye on the clock, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must try and have this evidence finished by the adjournment, and that includes the additional matter. I don't know how long you're going to be with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got five more questions, I think, maybe six.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first question. You said that preparation for Ahmici might be half a day. If, and it's for the Chamber to decide, of course, there were co-ordinated attacks on more than one target, does that time for preparation increase?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked whether you were speaking just from memory about the Kordic interview of the 26th of April, it was suggested you hadn't recorded it earlier. In your statement of 1995, you gave the same account. You set out at page 7 his reaction and you said when you gave your reaction, that he was subdued and concerned about the safety of himself. "He suggested I go to Jelinak and Putis because he claimed there was quite a Muslim offensive in progress. When I got there, things were relatively quiet." Do you stand by that passage set out in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I confirm that, in fact, Bosnian Croat houses had been destroyed in Putis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The 28th/29th of April convoy hijacking that is not referred to in your notes in any way, if a man -- did you know a man called Morsink, an ECMM monitor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If a monitor sought the assistance of one of your Warriors through another officer, was there any absolute need for that to come to your personal attention?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. If an ECMM man of any description sought assistance from any of my soldiers, that soldier was at liberty to give it, he made his own mind up. He didn't need to be an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An ultimate question, I think -- a penultimate question. May the 9th, the Blaskic and Kordic encounter, Blaskic saying he was in charge of the military, did he say that before or after Kordic arrived, or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: According to my diary, it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does his saying that have any significance for your judgement about the existence of external political supervision or influence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: No. As I explained at the start of my testimony, I believed there was kind of a joint command, political/military, and I don't see that that -- in the evidence I've given, I can't see any reason to change that, having revisited it in my mind over the last two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cerkez, did you know personally one way or another the degree of his involvement in the local command structure?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I think I've given evidence that I didn't -- I wasn't -- I'm not solid on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: I assumed him to be the commander of the HVO in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, when you spoke of Blaskic having overall authority and you gave the admiral on the ship analogy, where he was executing orders, by whom was he executing his orders or decisions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ALEXANDER STEWART
utterances.text: Of course. I mean, brigades must be commanded by the leaders or the commanders, and so orders sent down from Blaskic would be passed on through the brigade commanders. So there's the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see this piece of paper with the name on it. Please confirm without reading out the name that that is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In these proceedings, you'll be known as Witness AB. Witness AB, have you seen a summary of eight paragraphs setting out one or two matters relating to your involvement in these affairs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is what is said there by way of your background accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the preparation of a report, were you responding to requests from various people, ECMM, British Battalion, and others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the scope of the report, was there a request that you should effectively conduct a criminal investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A request that you speak into the microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a request that you conduct effectively a full criminal report --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- full criminal investigation? Your response to that being what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: The response was that we do not have the authority or the know-how to be able to conduct such an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the report you prepared was in accordance with your existing reporting practices and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, with those limitations, was the report prepared, to your knowledge, only contemporaneous and an independent report prepared at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: According to my information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you reviewed that report, have you reviewed your testimony in another case at this Tribunal, and are you in a position to adopt the report and your earlier testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I have and yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the report, with which the Chamber may be familiar from another witness, do you note that the terminology is specific and guarded with use of terms like "allegedly" and "reportedly"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You split the work between you, you and the other man, you dealing because of your background with Bosnian speaking witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So I come to just the two points that I want you to deal with. One, did you use a tape recorder at some stage to deal with witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The result?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: It was unsuccessful. The idea was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the tape not retained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second point. At the cinema in Zenica, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Muslims gathered following the atrocity in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A list or lists may have come into existence. First, was there a list of missing people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Originally there were 103 names, but that list at one point was then cut down to 101 names because two individuals from that list had been located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know how that list of 103 names was originally prepared or by whom it was prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I'm not really clear on who prepared the list, but it was presented to us as a list of missing from the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And presented, do you even now remember, by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No. No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perpetrators, was there a list, were there lists maybe of perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: There was a list of approximately 18 names. I think there were actually 18 names that were on a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Provided by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Once again, it wasn't on letterhead or anything like that which would indicate the source, and I really wouldn't know who provided it. It came at the same time as the list of the missing or shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That list, does it exist anymore, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you rely on it in your report to the extent of naming people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: The list was not reliable. It was a list that was presented to us without a source, and it really wouldn't be fair to name individuals from that list when we were not in a position to conduct an investigation or speak to anyone from that list and so on. So it wasn't something that we were involved in. And also, for the most part, we were not investigating perpetrators per se, it wasn't a part of our mandate to go to look for individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The names, we know, were supplied to Colonel Stewart as possibly involved in the massacre. Do you know where those names came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: We met often with Colonel Stewart. It's very possible that it came from us. We discussed many issues related to what we were doing with the Colonel, and it is very possible that in the course of those discussions he saw the list and actually even received the list from us. It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the names came from you, were they therefore, as it were, a subgroup of names coming from the 18 perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I would imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And subject to the same limitations, in your judgement, as any other name on that list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wonder if the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one matter, Mr. Sayers, before you begin. The report should be identified. My notes suggest this is Exhibit 942.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake for not having -- my oversight for not having dealt with that. Yes, Ms. Verhaag confirms it is 942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Good. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Witness AB, you gave testimony in another case in October of 1998, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I take it your recollection then was clearer than it is today, after the passage of a couple of years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher would simply put this page on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before we go to that passage, Witness AB, let me just correct a lack of courtesy on my part. My name is Stephen Sayers and I'm one of the attorneys who represents the accused Dario Kordic. Behind me are Mr. Kovacic and Mr. Mikulicic, and they represent the second accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez. Thank you. Two years ago when you were asked whether you gave any names to Colonel Stewart, your response was that you did not believe so, that you didn't think so, "No. No, I don't believe so." What has occurred in the intervening two years to change your testimony in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I have it in front of me, and actually line 9, it says, "I'm not sure. It's possible that something was handed over but I don't recollect any piece of paper," which is -- I still believe is the case. It was often in the evenings, after dinner or so, that we would sit and discuss many issues, including our fact-finding mission, and it is possible that during those conversations we discussed perpetrators. I think that there were those that were very interested in the names of perpetrators, and it very well could have come up as a topic. I don't recollect officially handing over a piece of paper and stating, "This is a list of perpetrators," no, that, I can't remember. But did it come up in a conversation? It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But you don't recall it coming up in a conversation, though, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No. No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you're not a trained criminal investigator yourself, are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe that your background is, you have a business degree from an American institution.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And you've never had any criminal investigation or forensic training at all, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Similarly, you've never had any military training, have you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What you were trying to do was to come up with factual findings, if you like, which would then be communicated to the Special Rapporteur, and your hope was that this would convince a government or an institution then to conduct a full-scale investigation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did such a full-scale investigation ever -- was it ever conducted by any government or any institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Other than the investigation that was conducted by the ICTY, I'm not aware of any other investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your mission, I believe, was to do a fact-finding exercise, and you were not instructed to do any kind of investigation at all, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: A fact-finding mission, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you consult anyone with professional criminal investigative techniques or forensic training in connection with the conduct of the fact-finding mission that you undertook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer. We were surrounded by officers from the British Battalion and other organisations in the field such as the ECMM and so on. We did ask questions of them. Yes, I would say we did consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. But you're not saying that the British soldiers to whom you spoke had any kind of criminal investigative training, or forensic training, or anything like that, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I would answer, no, I mean not specifically. But as being military personnel, they are knowledgeable in military issues, so they have ballistics and they know about military tactics and so on. I think that seeking out a specific expert, I think that was never done, but there are people that conveyed knowledge to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Witness AB, were you aware that, in fact, a forensic investigation was done of certain sites at Ahmici to determine whether any combustible accelerant substances such as petroleum had been used in the fighting in Ahmici on April the 16th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware that an analysis was done of the size or the calibre of shell casings found outside various houses in Ahmici on the 16th of April and conclusions were reached regarding the weapons type from which those weapons had been fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You met a number of individuals on various occasions. By my count, sir, and correct me if I'm wrong, you interviewed people at the cinema facility in Vitez on two separate occasions. I think that's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, two or even more. There was actually four -- I visited the cinema four different occasions, but I conducted interviews, yes, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You conducted interviews in the city of Zenica on two separate occasions as well. May the 2nd and May the 5th, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the cinema is in Zenica. I'm sorry. In the cinema building itself, that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The cinema building to which I spoke, maybe we're crossing --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you saying that your understanding is that the cinema building is in Zenica as opposed to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. I never visited the cinema building in Vitez. I automatically assumed that it was in Zenica. The only cinema that was visited was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The confusion is entirely mine, sir, and absolutely not your responsibility. My understanding is that on these four occasions when you were interviewing people who ultimately turned out to be eyewitnesses to some of the events about which this case is connected, you took contemporaneous notes. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: They are all lost, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: They were never retained. They are lost, yes, in fact they are lost. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the tape-recordings that you took, they are gone too, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself, in connection with the division of responsibilities averted to by counsel of the Prosecution, you yourself took onto your shoulders a responsibility for identifying people actually -- or interviewing people actually in the city of Zenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You yourself, therefore, did not actually interview anybody in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When you actually heard this errant tape-recording, the tape quality was very poor, there was lots of background noise, and in your view, the tape quality was virtually useless; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think, sir, there's no controversy about this. You spent a total of one week in Bosnia from April the 30th to May the 7th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, isn't it also true that you and your colleague got most of what information you were able to obtain about what had happened in Ahmici from the British army in various briefings and conversations with British army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Did you say "most"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I couldn't agree with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. From what other sources, other than the people that you've interviewed yourself in Zenica and the British army, did you acquire information about Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Well, there's the initial contact with the European Community Monitoring Mission. That was our first point of contact even before we deployed to the field, when they had requested that we do a criminal investigation. I think that -- well, there was a number of other sources; refugee -- UNHCR, High Commission for Refugees, there were interpreters, people that we met along the way. There is a number of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the perpetrators about which you were asked by the Prosecution, there was no way that you could have got those names from the Red Cross because the Red Cross, as I understand it, is prohibited from releasing information of that type. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I would agree. I don't think that I ever said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the same thing is true for the UNHCR; you never got any names --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your trying to find out some background information, you did, in fact, attend a fairly extensive briefing at the BritBat facility in Bila, just outside of Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That's the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't know those -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you spoke with a number of soldiers who had actually been on patrol in Ahmici on April the 16th; for example, then Lieutenant Wooley and then Lieutenant Dooley, correct, or do those names not ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Those names do ring a bell, but I believe that they were interviewed by my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And not by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Not by me, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. In that case, let's move on. Did you have available to you information or written reports from the European Community Monitoring Mission about which you or upon which you relied in order to gain an understanding as to the basic background of events that had occurred immediately prior to the dreadful events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: There was a report, but I believe that that report came much later, at a much later date. But I am aware of a report and I did read a report, but I don't believe that I read it while we were there or before we arrived. I think it came actually months later, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Just to cut through this, there is no other written documentation from the European Community Monitoring Mission or from the British army of which you're aware that you relied upon in preparing your interim report and ultimately the final report; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand it, you initially paid a visit to Ahmici during a trip around in an armoured fighting vehicle that was taking you all around the area, and the total trip lasted about two or three hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you had no communication with the tank commander, you were simply having things pointed out to you, but there was no dialogue as to the significance of what you were seeing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You did not see any houses on fire that day at all, did you? This is May the 1st, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't believe so, not in the village of Ahmici, but there were -- no, the answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. Let me turn to the interviews that you've described. The first one was at the cinema or a cinema building in Zenica, and it would be fair to say, sir, without any flourish or exaggeration, that that was a completely unproductive meeting, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The reason is because the people who you interviewed viewed you with intense suspicion, didn't they; they didn't trust you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Therefore, they didn't communicate any information substantively to you whatsoever, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, they were completely unwilling to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: There was a mass of people. It was very difficult to talk to anyone, and it was one of those things that you just have to give up on. It just would not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You paid a second visit to Ahmici, along with your colleague and representatives of the British army, I believe, some days later after May the 1st of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't recall anyone there from the British army, other than transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You took the opportunity yourself to tour around the area and were shot at by some unidentified soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you found, in Ahmici on that day, a burned green Muslim flag with Arabic writing on it, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You also found large quantities of spent shell casings in front of the destroyed houses, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And many bullet strike holes in the houses themselves visible to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And that's perfectly obvious to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the second visit that you paid to the cinema some time later. Can you recall approximately when it was, how many days later, or one day later, or you're just not able to remember after this large lapse of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, the second visit was -- let's see. It would be on the third or on the fourth day that we were with British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you had, during your second visit to Ahmici, picked up someone's identification card, and that was seen as imbuing you, if you like, with added reliability, and so people were prepared to speak with you, having seen that you had actually paid a visit to Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, sir, that on this second occasion you interviewed 12 to 15 people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And there were lots of children running in and out of the interview. It wasn't a particularly useful situation in order to conduct formal interviews with these people, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Not particularly good, good circumstances, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Can you recall, sir, in connection with the 18 names that you identified, was it on this second visit to the cinema that you were given this list of 18 names or that these 18 names were given to you, or do you just not remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I wonder if I could just ask the usher to put this document on the ELMO, and I would just like to ask you if this is, indeed, the list of 18 names that you referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I really can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. And in your view, it's impossible to authenticate any such lists -- thank you, Mr. Usher, we're done with that. You simply cannot remember who gave it to you or where it came from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Sir, we were given a document that appears to be dated May the 2nd, 1993, that appears to be typewritten summaries of interviews that apparently you conducted. Do you recall seeing that document in the recent past?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that document. I'm not sure it's interviews conducted by me. There were three attempts at transcribing the tapes -- the tape that I tried to make at the cinema in Zenica. I'm aware of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's also a map that you were -- that was attached to the documents that you were given. Do you recall seeing that map at all? I'll have it put on the ELMO, if I may. Thank you. I wonder if we could --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this document, this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who gave you this map, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I believe it's a photocopy that I had made from a newspaper or a journal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And this was during your trip to Zenica in early May of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if we could just increase the scale of the magnification, please. Is that possible? Actually, no, the other way. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, there are a number of black arrows that are showing right at the top of the picture there, two pointed towards Vitez and to the east of Vitez, two pointed essentially either side of Busovaca. And according to the legend, it says, "Direction of BH army attack." Did you ever have any discussions about this particular map or plan with anybody, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with the interviews that you conducted in Zenica on May the 2nd, 1993, you asked whether there were any armed forces in Ahmici, and you were told that there were a few but very few; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: According to the survivors that you interviewed, all of the soldiers were wearing normal camouflage HVO uniforms and none of them were actually wearing black uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't remember, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you a statement from an interim report that's already in evidence, Your Honour. This was prepared by Witness AB and the other witness. It's Exhibit D66/1, and on page 6 of that interim report, which you participated in writing, did you not, Witness AB --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: If that's the document, I would imagine so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Maybe it would be better if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Witness AB, this document doesn't have any page numbers on it, but if you could turn to the sixth page, I think that's the one I'm interested in. It says: "The team did not receive any eyewitness accounts of their involvement in atrocities --" Sorry. "Because of their distinctive black uniform, soldiers belonging to HOS can be easily distinguished from HVO or other soldiers." And you did not receive any reports, as far as you can remember, of any of these distinctive black uniforms being seen by any of the eyewitness survivors in Ahmici, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That's page 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. It's about four or five inches up or five inches up from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: I don't understand the context of the whole question. I'm a bit confused. How does it relate to this report and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's entirely my fault. You do not recall any of your eyewitnesses survivors telling you that they saw people wearing black uniforms in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the only point I wanted to make. Now, sir, several of the people you interviewed mentioned that there had been shelling on the morning of April the 16th, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, this was a fairly consistent theme in the reports that you received from the eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS AB
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
